scenes.title: Top N Queries
scenes.narration: Top N queries answer a common analytics question: which are the highest-ranking rows, either overall or within each group.

scenes.title: Global top N versus top N per group

left.title: Global top N
points: One ranked list across the whole table
ORDER BY the metric, then LIMIT N

right.title: Top N per group
points: A separate top list inside each group
Needs a window function to rank within partitions

scenes.narration: There are two flavors of this problem. Global top N is a single ranked list over the entire table, which you get by ordering on the metric and applying LIMIT. Top N per group is harder: you want a separate ranking inside each category, which a plain LIMIT cannot do. For that you need a window function that ranks rows within partitions and then a filter on the rank.

scenes.title: Global top 5 products by revenue
scenes.code:
SELECT product_id, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM sales
GROUP BY product_id
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 5;
scenes.narration: The global case is straightforward. We aggregate total revenue per product with SUM and GROUP BY, order the result by revenue in descending order so the biggest sellers come first, and LIMIT to five rows. That gives us the five highest-grossing products across the entire sales table.

scenes.title: Top 3 products per category
scenes.code:
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT
        category,
        product_id,
        SUM(amount) AS revenue,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY category
            ORDER BY SUM(amount) DESC
        ) AS rn
    FROM sales
    GROUP BY category, product_id
)
SELECT category, product_id, revenue
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= 3
ORDER BY category, revenue DESC;
scenes.narration: For top N per group we use a window function inside a CTE. We compute revenue per product per category, then ROW_NUMBER partitioned by category and ordered by revenue descending numbers the products within each category, so the top seller in every category gets rank one. In the outer query we simply keep the rows where that rank is three or less. The result is the three best products for each category, all in one pass.

scenes.title: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, or DENSE_RANK?
bullets: ROW_NUMBER: always unique, breaks ties arbitrarily to give exactly N rows
RANK: ties share a rank and leave gaps, so ties can exceed N
DENSE_RANK: ties share a rank with no gaps in the numbering
Choose based on how you want to handle tied metrics
scenes.narration: Which ranking function you pick matters when metrics tie. ROW_NUMBER always assigns distinct numbers, breaking ties arbitrarily so you get exactly N rows. RANK gives tied rows the same number and then skips ahead, so a three-way tie for first jumps to rank four and you may return more than N rows. DENSE_RANK also shares ranks on ties but leaves no gaps. Choose based on whether tied rows should all be included.

scenes.text: For top N per group, rank inside a partition with a window function, then filter on the rank in an outer query. LIMIT alone cannot do per-group tops.
scenes.narration: The pattern to remember is: rank within a partition using a window function, then filter on that rank in an outer query, because a plain LIMIT can never give you a top list per group.
